entries.meaning: Bṛhaspati said that service to Sītā’s Lord by one of his servants is as lovely as a hundred wish-fulfilling cows. ‘Devotion to Bharata has arisen in your minds; abandon anxiety, for destiny has arranged the matter. See Bharata’s power, king of gods: Raghurāya is naturally subject to his disposition. Steady your mind and do not fear; know Bharata as Rāma’s shadow.’ Hearing his guru’s divinely approved thought, the all-knowing Lord felt reserve. Bharata understood that the burden rested on his own head and formed millions of conjectures within. Reflecting, he settled his mind: Rāma’s command was the good he should choose. ‘He abandoned his own vow to preserve mine and has shown no small compassion and love.’ Sītānātha had bestowed boundless grace upon him in every way. Bharata bowed and spoke, joining his two lotus hands.

Bharata said: ‘What can I say or cause to be said now, master, ocean of compassion and knower of hearts? The guru is pleased and my master favorable; the imagined spears in my defiled mind have vanished. I am free of inward fear and anxiety at the root: when the quarters go astray, the fault lies not in the sun. My misfortune, my mother’s crookedness, destiny’s strange course, and the harshness of time all planted their feet and hurled me down; but the protector of the surrendered kept his own vow. This is not a new custom for you, and neither world nor Veda keeps it hidden. One Lord makes the world’s ill turn good—whose goodness could produce such good? God and the divine tree share this nature: neither asks whether one approaches rightly or wrongly. At the tree’s shade every anxiety is calmed; near it king and pauper, good and bad, obtain whatever they seek.’

‘Seeing in every way the guru’s and master’s love, my agitation and doubt have disappeared. Compassionate Lord, now do what will serve the people without troubling your heart. A servant who makes his master hesitate while seeking personal benefit has a corrupt understanding. True service is for the master’s good; it abandons greed for every comfort. Everyone’s practical welfare lies in your return, Lord, and carrying out your command is good in a million ways. It is the essence of worldly and highest good, fruit of all merit, and adornment of the blessed path. Lord, hear one request; afterward do with it whatever is fitting. The complete equipment for consecration has been brought—if your heart agrees, make it fruitful. Send me with Śatrughna into the forest and give everyone a protector; otherwise send both brothers back and I shall accompany you.’

Bharata added: ‘Or else let all three brothers go to the forest and Raghurāya return with Sītā. Compassionate ocean, do whatever will make your heart pleased. My lord has given me the whole burden, but I retain no deliberation about policy or duty. Every word I speak seeks my own interest; a distressed person’s mind keeps no awareness. A servant who gives an answer after hearing the master’s command feels shame when he recognizes his conduct. Though I am this unfathomable ocean of defects, saints praise me because of the master’s love. Compassionate Lord, I now accept whatever judgment leaves no reserve in my master’s mind. By your feet I swear that I speak truly: there is one way for the world’s welfare. If you gladly abandon reserve and give each person an order, everyone will bear it upon the head and carry it out; confusion and embarrassment will vanish.’

The gods rejoiced at Bharata’s pure words; saints praised him and gods showered flowers. Ayodhyā’s inhabitants remained in uncertainty, while the forest ascetics were glad. Raghunātha fell silent through reserve and the assembly worried upon seeing the Lord’s condition. At that moment Janaka’s messengers arrived; hearing of them, sage Vasiṣṭha quickly summoned them. They bowed and gazed upon Rāma; seeing his ascetic dress, they became deeply distressed. The eminent sage asked: ‘Tell me, is King Videha well?’ The excellent envoys bowed to earth with joined hands and replied hesitantly: ‘Lord, to ask us respectfully is itself the reason any welfare remains. Otherwise well-being departed with the lord of Kosala; Mithilā and Ayodhyā especially—and indeed the whole world—have been orphaned.’

The envoys recounted that when news of the lord of Kosala’s fate reached Janaka’s city, all its people went mad with grief. Whoever saw Videha then felt the name ‘bodiless’ no longer true of him. Hearing the queen’s plot, the king could see nothing, like a serpent deprived of its jewel. Bharata’s enthronement and Raghubara’s exile struck Mithilā’s lord like terror in the heart. Janaka asked his wise ministers what was proper; understanding Ayodhyā’s double uncertainty, none could say whether he should go or remain. Steadying himself, the king sent four clever spies to Ayodhyā: ‘Learn Bharata’s true or false disposition and return quickly without being detected.’ The agents went, discovered Bharata’s condition and conduct, and left for Citrakūṭa alongside Bharata’s party; Janaka departed from Tirhut when his four returned.

The messengers related Janaka’s actions and condition as best they could. Hearing, guru, family, ministers, and kings became deeply overwhelmed by anxiety and love. Janaka had steadied himself, praised Bharata, summoned warriors and commanders, appointed guardians for house, city, and country, and prepared many horses, elephants, and chariots. Setting out at once after arranging a two-watch journey, the king did not rest along the way. Early that morning he had bathed at Prayāga and was now crossing the Yamunā with everyone. ‘You sent us for news, Lord,’ the envoys concluded, bowing their heads to earth. The sage gave them six or seven Kirāta guides and immediately dismissed them. Hearing of Janaka’s approach, Ayodhyā’s entire company rejoiced; Raghunandana felt great reserve, while Indra was overcome by anxiety.

Crooked Kaikeyī melted with shame; whom could she tell, and upon whom lay the blame? Men and women took heart and rejoiced at the thought that they would remain four more days. That day passed in this way, and in the morning everyone began to bathe. Men and women immersed themselves, then worshiped Gaṇeśa, Gaurī, Tripurāri, and Sūrya. Bowing next to the feet of Lakṣmī’s Lord, they petitioned with joined palms and garment-ends: ‘May Rāma be king, Jānakī queen, and Ayodhyā the boundless capital of joy. May he return with the company and dwell there happily; Rāma, make Bharata crown prince. Water everyone with this nectar of happiness, gods, and grant the world the gain of life. May Rāma reign in the city with guru, assembly, and brothers. While Rāma is alive, may everyone ask to die in Ayodhyā with Rāma as king.’

Hearing the citizens’ loving speech, even ascetic sages of knowledge disparaged yoga and detachment. After completing their daily rites, the citizens bowed to Rāma with thrilled bodies. High, low, and middling men and women obtained his sight according to their particular station. He attentively honored everyone, and all praised the abode of grace. Since childhood Raghubara had recognized and upheld policy and affection in his speech; Raghurāya was an ocean of conduct and reserve, with lovely face and eyes and simple nature. Speaking his many virtues in love, people praised their own fortune: ‘Few in the world possess a heap of merit like ours, whom Rāma knows as his own.’ As all were absorbed in love, news came that the lord of Mithilā approached. Rāma, sun to the lotuses of the Solar line, rose respectfully with the assembly.

With brothers, ministers, guru, and citizens, Raghunātha went forward to meet Janaka. As soon as Janaka saw the great mountain, he bowed and left his chariot. His longing and eagerness for Rāma’s sight erased every trace of road weariness or pain. His mind was where Raghubara and Vaidehī were; without the mind, how could the body register pleasure or pain? Thus Janaka advanced with the company, his understanding intoxicated by love. Drawing near, both sides saw each other’s attachment and began exchanging respectful greetings. Janaka bowed at the sages’ feet; Raghunandana saluted the seers. Rāma and his brothers met the king and led him onward with his whole party. The hermitage was an ocean full of peaceful rasa and sacred water, and Raghunātha seemed to bring toward it rivers of compassion in the form of the armies.
